7. A Chinook salmon can jump out of water with a speed \(v_0\) and an angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal. What is the speed of the fish when it is at the maximum height?
A. \(v_0\).
B. \(v_0 \cos \theta\).
C. \(v_0 \sin \theta\).
D. 0.
datasource_item.generated_question_text:
Q7. A soccer ball is kicked with a launch speed \(v_0\) at an angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal (neglect air resistance). What is the speed of the ball at its maximum height?
A. \(v_0\)
This ignores that the vertical component of velocity decreases to zero at the top.
B. \(v_0\cos\theta\)
At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero, so the speed equals the unchanged horizontal component \(v_0\cos\theta\).
C. \(v_0\sin\theta\)
This confuses the initial vertical component with the speed at the peak, where the vertical component is actually zero.
D. 0
Only the vertical component becomes zero at the top; the horizontal component remains nonzero.

1. Which of the following statements is correct?
A. We can assume a "spherical cow" when analyzing the motion of a cow's leg.
B. We can safely assume a cow is a point mass when analyzing its position change in the scale of a mile over a certain time period.
C. We can never assume the cow is in a vacuum, even when we need to ignore the effect of air resistance.
D. None of the above is correct.

A. We can model a hummingbird’s wing as a point mass when predicting the detailed bending motion during a wingbeat.
This confuses whole-body motion modeling with the need for an extended-body model to capture wing deformation.
B. We can model a city bus as a point mass when tracking its position change over several kilometers on a map.
Over kilometer-scale travel the bus’s size is negligible compared with the distance, so a point-mass model is appropriate.
C. We are never allowed to treat the surroundings as a vacuum, even if we intend to neglect air drag in a calculation.
This is incorrect because “vacuum” is often used as an idealization to ignore air resistance when it is negligible.
D. None of the above statements is correct.
Option B is a valid modeling approximation, so “none” is not correct.

Q10. An object can escape a planet with radius R and mass M at an escape speed given by \(v=\sqrt{2GM/R}\), where G is the universal gravitational constant. Based on this expression for escape speed, which of the following statements is correct?
A. A more massive spacecraft needs a larger escape speed from the same planet.
The spacecraft’s mass does not appear in \(v=\sqrt{2GM/R}\), so escape speed is independent of the object’s mass.
B. If a planet’s radius increases while its mass stays the same, the escape speed increases.
Since \(v\propto 1/\sqrt{R}\), increasing R actually decreases the escape speed when M is fixed.
C. A planet with smaller mass and larger radius requires a higher escape speed.
Both smaller M and larger R reduce M/R, so they lower the escape speed rather than raise it.
D. A planet with greater mass and smaller radius requires a higher escape speed.
Because \(v\propto \sqrt{M/R}\), increasing M and decreasing R both increase M/R and thus increase v.

A. The moving distance is 7.8 m.
B. The speed at t = 0 must be 2.6 m/s.
C. The acceleration at t = 0 must be 0.87 m/s2
D. None of the above is correct.
datasource_item.generated_question_text:
Q6. An object takes 4 seconds to move from position A (\(\vec{r}_A=1.0\hat{\imath}-3.0\hat{\jmath}\)) to position B (\(\vec{r}_B=-5.0\hat{\imath}+4.0\hat{\jmath}\)) along a straight path, where length units are in meters. Which of the following statements is correct?
A. The moving distance is 9.2 m.
For straight-line travel the distance equals \(|\Delta\vec{r}|=\sqrt{(-6)^2+7^2}=\sqrt{85}\approx 9.2\) m.
B. The speed at t = 0 must be 2.3 m/s.
Knowing only endpoints and total time does not uniquely determine the initial speed without a motion model.
C. The acceleration at t = 0 must be 0.58 m/s2.
Acceleration cannot be inferred from just the endpoints and elapsed time without additional information about the trajectory in time.
D. None of the above is correct.
Option A is correct because the straight-line distance is determined solely by the endpoints.
